title: Studying Religion Fairly
objective: After this level you can explain how scholars describe what believers hold without judging whether it is true, and why no faith speaks with a single voice.
summary: Scholars bracket the question of truth to describe religions in their own terms; 'myth' in their usage means a sacred story, not a false one; and every tradition is a family of subtraditions.

cards.headline: Can you explain a faith accurately without deciding if it's true?
cards.body: Scholars of religion try to do exactly that. Here's the method, a word that trips people up, and the reason no religion ever speaks with just one voice.

cards.headline: Put truth in brackets
cards.body: Scholars in the phenomenology of religion use a technique called epoché: "bracketing", or suspending judgment. They set aside their own beliefs to describe a religion in its own terms, with empathy for the people who practice it. The question "is it true?" isn't thrown away. It's set aside so the description comes out fair. A believer and a skeptic should both be able to read it and nod.

cards.headline: A myth isn't a mistake
cards.body: Scholars often call a religion's sacred stories myths, and that word trips people up. In everyday speech a myth is something false. In the study of religion, Smart explained, calling a story a myth carries no implication that it is false. And to believers, he added, these narratives are very often history. So when a scholar says "myth", read "sacred story", nothing more.

cards.headline: No faith speaks with one voice
cards.body: Smart asked readers to picture a Baptist chapel in Georgia, plain, with hymns, Bible reading and fervent preaching, and an Eastern Orthodox church in Romania, glowing with candles and icons, full of processions and chanting. Both are Christian, and both feel like home to their members. Every tradition, Smart wrote, is a loosely held-together family of subtraditions.

mascot.line: When you hear "all Christians" or "all Hindus believe", slow down. "Many" or "most" is usually closer to the truth.

cards.headline: Studying Religion Fairly: the takeaways
learned: Scholars bracket the question of truth to describe religions fairly
In the study of religion, a myth is a sacred story, not a false one
Every tradition is a family of subtraditions

questions.prompt: Scholars of religion call setting aside the question of a faith's truth _____.

options.label: apologetics, defending a faith
options.rationale: That argues for a faith rather than bracketing.

questions.explanation: Phenomenologists use epoché, bracketing or suspending judgment, to describe religions in their own terms.

questions.prompt: Match each term or place with what this level says about it.
questions.explanation: Epoché means suspending judgment, and a myth means a sacred story. Smart's Baptist chapel in Georgia has fervent preaching; the Orthodox church in Romania glows with candles and icons.

questions.prompt: Smart's plain Baptist chapel and candlelit Orthodox church differ most visibly in which of Level 3's dimensions?

options.label: Doctrine and ethics
options.rationale: Both are Christian in doctrine; the visible gap is worship and objects.

questions.explanation: Hymns and preaching versus processions and chanting is ritual; plain walls versus candles and icons is material.
